question: What was the Edict of Milan (313 AD) and why is it significant?

choices.A: An agreement between emperors Constantine and Licinius granting religious tolerance to all in the Roman Empire, ending systematic persecution of Christians
choices.B: Constantine's decree declaring Christianity the official and only religion of the Roman Empire
choices.C: A council decree defining the Nicene Creed
choices.D: The founding document of the Papal States, granting the pope temporal authority over central Italy

teaching.title: The Edict of Milan (313)
teaching.body: The Edict of Milan was a letter of toleration issued by Constantine I and Licinius in 313 AD, granting freedom of religion to all within the Roman Empire and specifically ending the persecution of Christians that had culminated under Diocletian (303-311). It restored confiscated church property and allowed Christians to worship openly. It did not make Christianity the state religion — that came later under Theodosius I (Edict of Thessalonica, 380). The Edict of Milan marks the end of the era of martyrdom and the beginning of the Constantinian era.
